text:
CORRECTION: We're working on updating the video, but in the meantime, our numbers for Cyberpunk 2077 were with FidelityFX Upscaling enabled. We specifically didn't have this enabled, but stability issues with the bench seems to have messed with the settings. We've re-run all of the numbers for each card:

*No RT, no DLSS (1%low, 5%low, avg):
- RTX 4090: 54, 69, 81
- RTX 3090 Ti: 43, 46, 56
- RTX 3090: 35, 43, 50
- RX 6950 XT: 30, 39, 46

*RT, no DLSS (1%low, 5%low, avg):
- RTX 4090: 36, 39, 44
- RTX 3090 Ti: 17, 22, 26
- RTX 3090: 16, 19, 23
- RX 6950 XT: 10, 11, 13

*RT + DLSS (1%low, 5%low, avg):
- RTX 4090: 94, 97, 108
- RTX 3090 Ti: 58, 60, 67
- RTX 3090: 52, 53, 61
- RX 6950 XT: N/A

-AY

text:
Anythony is just so awesome, like fr every one of us gamers and tech enthusiasts out there knows he's among the GOATs for listening to on unbiased hardware reviews, like him and Steve. I think HWUB can be pretty good too, but I understand why some may say upside down Steve is too pro-red (although, in all frankness, it's pretty damn easy to see why considering EVGA dropped their asses and they had the audacity to threaten him for not emphasizing raytacing enough, it's literally almost 2023 on 3rd gen RTX and I still don't really give a F about RT much).

Oh, and btw, it's ok to have strong opinion and still be unbiased. Like I don't think his review on Macshit was biased. We just all know that Apple sucks. I think some people get really confused about our societies (fatburgers in particular) in thinking that just because one vote=1 vote, and just because we allegedly have equal rights and free speech and all that, and that reporters are supposed to be unbiased, they come to a few erroneous conclusions:
1) that in order to be a journalist, or host any kind of debate, or be unbiased generally, you have to give equal screenspace to the other opinions no matter how outlandish.
This is horse shit. Just because your schizophrenic friend believes that the ancient Atlanteans used a portal to put a flag on the moon, doesn't mean ANYONE let alone a respectable journalist is in any way obligated to give your utter horse shit pants on head retarded psychotic opinion even a pretense of equal consideration. In point of fact, clinical psychopaths do this shit on purpose by issuing the most outlandish opinion they possibly can (like say, agitating for building death camps for black people) in order to get allegedly "reasonable" people to give their viciously stupid, psychopathic ideas more credit to agree to "meet in the middle" and "only" build a few death camps for some people. The very existence of those ideas is why journalists should go even harder in rejecting them. Like trying to act like nVidia pricing "isn't that unreasonable" yes, yes it f'ing is.

2) that all ideas are created equal. This is equally bullshit, for the aforementioned reasons. It doesn't matter if it's commonly held, it doesn't matter if it's a rumour, and it sure as shit doesn't matter that you also get one vote. The idea in voting and free speech, btw, is that some idea so outlandishly retarded, like saying Dell makes good hardware, is that the rest of people who actually have a clue will speak up freely and refute you, and that the actually reasonable, sane, or informed people would average out the psychotic psychopathic nutjobs that are sincerely pushing for things like starting a civil war, storing your most precious data on only one drive, or giving Apple and nVidia your money right now. Ideas are not created equal, and not all cultures are good ones. I really don't care that it's somebody else's insane, retarded idea, Bacha Bazai boy parties are inferior and disgusting, Dixie Klan culture is inferior to my own, and "alienware" hasn't truly existed since Dell eviscerated that company.

Obviously, Anthony is not going to agree with all I'm saying, nor should that be implied, but I'm just saying, that I like Anthony for those reasons and find him trustworthy the same way I find Steve trustworthy: because he isn't full of shit and he's willing to say what's wrong, and I don't feel like his arse is up for sale. He's funny and he's a good man, I trust his character. He's willing to just say what's what, and you can trust a person because they actually know what they're talking about and are just trying to get you the most accurate information possible. This is why Steve and Anthony are among my favourite journalists. I don't feel like they'll compromise themselves, and we're all sick of the price gouging b.s. of these companies and people in power with tons of money when all the little ol me's just want to get a graphics card to play games on (I realize the irony of saying it for this video, but I came here looking to bitch about power consumption.)

text:
Why did Nvidia Market the 40 series without DP2.0?

"DisplayPort 2.1 specs released, just before AMD unleashes RDNA 3 GPUs
VESA announces the new DisplayPort 2.1 standard, is a newer, more demanding DP2.1 spec that arrive with up to 80Gbps of bandwidth for 4K240 and 8K120

Published Oct 17, 2022 5:55 PM CDT
VESA has just announced the updated DisplayPort 2.1 specification today, also announcing that any DisplayPort 2.0-ready product is now a DisplayPort 2.1-certified product.... and those products do NOT include NVIDIA's new GeForce RTX 40 series GPUs (unfortunately, and very silly I might add).

AMD has its new Ryzen 6000 series with DisplayPort 2.0 compatibility, as well as Intel's did-they-even-release-it Arc A770 and Arc A750 graphics cards have DP2.0 ports, which have now all been silently upgraded to DP2.1 overnight. NVIDIA's new GeForce RTX 4090 does NOT have DisplayPort 2.0, so there's no upgrade to DisplayPort 2.1, which is something that I've covered extensively before, during, and after the RTX 4090 launch."

text:
I’m glad someone is finally talking about this, well done.  Sticking with 1.4a for a third generation in a row when DP 2.0 has been out for over 3 years is an odd way to cheap-out on a very expensive card.  In addition to 8K displays and high-refresh 4K HDR displays needing the extra bandwidth, and the 4090 being able to make use of it,  higher resolution & refresh rate VR headsets are on the way, such as the Pimax 12K (6K each eye, reportedly 200 Hz) that would certainly benefit from DP 2.0.  

Reports today also allege that AMD’s RDNA 3 cards will not just support DP 2.0 as previously reported, but may support DP 2.1 (which hasn’t yet been publicly announced).  Things should get interesting soon.  I’m holding off to see RDNA3 vs 4000 series head-to-head real-world benchmark comparisons before I buy.

text:
A controversial take - I agree with the 4090 price. Not the 4080 and the other "4080". 

I'd love to have a conversation about it in the comments if you can spell something other than "fuck nvidia". I'd like to hear someone else's opinion as well. 

Nvidia did deliver on the performance uplift, they improved dlss (which in time will be key upgrade for slower cards like 4050 on next gen titles, especially on cpu bound games at 1080p), outstanding thermal conductivity on the reference card and all the less but still important things like so much better tensor cores, much more and better SMs, double AV1 encoder and decoder - all this while not taking a single step backwards and rising the price by a meager hundred dollars, which is negligible if you have the budget for this kind of hardware. Especially after taking inflation into account. 

There's pressure on nvidia and it tries to deliver. They bought more wafers because of the gpu shortage, now the roles are reversed and there's an oversupply, so of course they need to raise the prices of the newer gen to keep selling older cards to sell through them. They also can't improve things out of thin air. You just can't expect to get 20% uplift at the same price every 2 years. 




We got a top-notch card at a high, but justified price. Older generations are still available with declining price, because we're all not expected to be able to afford it. The cards are built to last and even the older cards' drivers are still being updated.

text:
I'm going to be upgrading my system to AM5, so this time around I'm going to rid of any 2.5" drives and just utilize two M.2 NVME 4.0 SSD's to rid of un-needed cables. For me it seems like no matter how good my case is I have some random cable running from something that I have to cram somewhere to get it out of the way. Since NVME ssd's are more reasonably priced now I'm going to replace my current 500GB M.2 SSD system drive with a 1TB and my current 2.5" SATA 2TB game storage SSD with a 2TB NVME drive just to clean things up more.

 In my opinion, with how pricey the newer platforms are becoming being able to run multiple NVME M.2 drives directly on the board and having them cleanly out of the way and unseen should be the norm. Get rid of the clunky old SATA ports all together as till having to run cables out of the way is pointless. Some might try to debate saying they need the 2.5" drives and SATA ports but in actuality you don't if you have a good motherboard that can hide away 4 M.2 drives under its' heatsinks. Then you have more premium boards from MSI and ASUS that give you PCI cards for adding another 4 M.2 drives on top of that. So ya, the old SATA ports are rather pointless.

As for the 4090, I'm seriously considering one this time around and have no problems with saving the funds for it. But I am still going to wait before hand as I would like to see what AMD's 7000 cards are going to be like. If they offer performance even remotely close to this I'll just stick with AMD as I always have. As for current offerings, I'm still going to purchase a 6900/6950XT when prices fall further just in case we have another stupid shortage again that seems to be the norm each year.

text:
Here's a question for DLSS 3.0.
So, let say the graphics card can rendered 30 FPS at native. Then DLSS kicked in, now it renders at a lower resolution, as a result, it now produce 45 FPS.
Now, DLSS 3.0 add frames in between in those 45 FPS, now it becomes 90 FPS. My question is who did the work for those extra FPS? Fake or not, it still needs to be rendered, even worse, now it needs to guess what should happen in between. How did the GPU found extra performance to add those fake frames?

If my guess is correct, then it is the CPU that did the work for those fake frames. So basically, DLSS 3.0 is a scam, the CPU did the work but the GPU claimed the credit. And that's probably why everybody is reporting CPU bottleneck at 4K.

text:
Not sure about the video title, I feel like the fastest possible GPU absolutely is always objectively best. If you can power and cool it (and your CPU can keep up or you run higher resolutions), then yes. A component measured purely on speed and performance should be as fast and powerful as possible.

Obviously very small form factor builds, people with any kind of budget limitations or those with weak PSUs or low res displays probably wouldn't want/need one but if you can run it, then the fastest is always best.

That all said, I've been sick of Nvidia for ages banging on about RT performance, DLSS figures etc. when until the 4090 it's been basically irrelevant. Very few people on a 3060 are going to turn on RT and sacrifice half their framerate for some more accurate window reflections, especially when they're blurry as hell thanks to heavy DLSS.
I run a 3080 and even I don't use high RT settings in basically anything, in fact I rarely have it turned on at all since it doesn't add a whole lot and the performance hit is massive

text:
What is most impressive about 40s series, is DLSS 3 capability to ML predict additional frames. That really changes what DLSS is, as in that case it isn't a compromise in quality anymore, even a worthy one. It is just plain better, and honestly gets to the point where turning DLSS off in a benchmark becomes unrealistic, as it will have more FPS with it while without the old DLSS features rendering on the same resolution and quality. Heck you could use DLSS old features to render at higher quality & resolution, and still get more FPS.
I am surprised that few of the reviewers have paid much attention to it. Don't get me wrong, not going to run out and buy one for that now, but as games support gets added, it is a real world beater.

text:
its competition.  The 20 series might not have been as much of an improvement because nVidia ballooned the size of their chips in order to fit in all the extra RT/Tensor stuff, but the 30 series returned more to normalcy, however actual threat of competition from AMD lead them to be as aggressive as possible with performance with less regard for how power they are targeting per tier.

Power/performance has never really gotten worse since the 10 series, you just have to be willing to apply your own limits to the cards.  Take a 2080, tune it to draw no more power than a 1080, it will still be plenty faster.  The 3080, even more so.

What will be really interesting to see is the 12GB "4080", which has a die size smaller than the 1080 (and is barely larger than a 3050/60), but has more transistors than a 3090 Ti.  Its just a major shame they're trying to fleece us for it with that absurd $900 MSRP.

text: Really nVidia is correct that the 4090 isn't going up against a throughput bottleneck for gaming and/or any normal GPU compute loads. So unless you bought it as a replacement for a " low end" GPU compute card PCIe gen 4 should be enough. You also have the extra heat from the PCIe gen 5 controller would need to go some where and the extra power it will need to run properly. PCIe gen 5 controllers are also new and untested to put onto an expensive product. Remember how the M.2 drives gen 3 to gen 4 did before the gen 4 chip got better? Using a PCIe gen 5 chip would do the same reducing performance. Most likely the 5090 will have it with a new PCIe gen 5 controller chip that will give better performance than the PCIe gen 4 controller chip would.

There are some games that have hard software created caps (Fallout 4, Skyrim, Lost Planet 3, Assassin's Creed IV, many of your fighting games SoulCalibur VI, etc) that will start doing all kinds of goofy often enough game breaking things if you try to unlock it.  As near as I can recall the games on the list in this video have no such limiter.

So, the variances noted should, in theory, come down to room temperatures, case (if used) and difference in system parts (motherboard, CPU, RAM would potentially make the biggest differences) rather than monitor used.
I could pontificate further but I think you get the picture.

text:
only having the old version of display port is indeed heavily problematic for gamers which the PCIE4 might be problematic for content creators.
If they want to save money then why not do it like old laptops used to do it, just have one output or 2 outputs for DisplayPort 2 and use the others for displayport 1, even if those ports with displayport 2 where made without backwars compatibility to possibly save a few cents that would still be great, since for high end gaming you need DisplayPort, since that is the only widely used video port standard that can handle such high data rates at high speed and low latency. adding the newest version of display port would certainly be something you would desire on a GPU labeled for gaming.
well luckily they still have displayport 1, however if they didn't have it could have made the joke of: "what do they expect us to connect our gaming monitors to?, hdmi?" for those who don't know: HDMI basically almost completely voids the reason why you would want high refresh rates coming from your gpu. a screen having a high refreshrate is logic, but the GPU only needs to deliver fast enough that you don't see the frames anymore, the only reason you would want it higher is to prevent latency and such so you get the input more directly, in HDMI that last reason is mostly void since it can't relyably do that at high resolution since HDMI is super old and was esigned for watching movies and such, not for gaming or low latency and stability in that latency. HDMI is also propetairy and so not open which results in a lot of problems, unstability, security problems, etc. HDMI still is great as a general video output however, atleast as long as you aren't troubled by their propetairy nature and you directly needing to pay a decent licencing fee(included in product price) just to licence that hdmi port(HDMI licencing is per port, and is actually quite expensive when we look to small devices like the lower budged raspberry pi models where HDMI port licencing actually is a rather large part of the price the eventual custommers pay to buy the device). but if you need something more modern with low and relyable latency and with many things you can change/configure and with high data rates then display port is what you need.

To those complaining that the top of the line card is too expensive…

This product is not for the mass market but for the enthusiast. PC gaming is no longer an enthusiast market reserved only for hardcore gamers. It’s mainstream. 

The boom in popularity for PC gaming has increased research and development budgets and now we have tech that guys like me who started back in the days when the GTX 280 came out, yes 280 lol was a massive jump. Even then I was considered to be apart of new wave of mainstream gamers. 

Gaming PCs where stupid expensive back then and had 1 percent of the power we have today combined with the fact that we had .01 percent of the games available today that were only available on hard disks. I would argue that gaming back then was even more expensive and less of a value then it is today. 
Times have changed and this card is meant for the guy who would justify $2300 for a low-mid range bang for the buck pc setup in 2008 vs a $300 Xbox 360 only to still have realistically the same performance… 30fps 1080p expect across all of our games. 

The goal post has moved closer in my opinion. 

You are right about this still being unattainable for the price, but you gotta pay to play if you wanna stay in the cutting edge.

text:
Honestly, this.

I have a shunt modded 2080ti (basically within 15% of a 3080), and it only drives about half the titles acceptably in VR sim racing.  (There are even compromises in Project CARS 2.)

With the ~3x improvement this represents, I'm expecting to actually be able to supersample for extra clarity, and to be able to run Assetto Corsa Competizione at full frame rates with no DLSS (deferred renderers suck).

It's also no contest for nvenc for roomscale when streaming wirelessly.

If the next generation VR headsets were going to be DP2.0, I would agree on the omission sucking.  But I also expect that they will continue to be wireless ala Quest 2/Pico Neo/Pimax Crystal.

Let's see what AMD brings to the table, but I'm expecting worse everything, even raster.
author: @pondracek

text: @pondracek  Such a shame that so little new headsets use displayport. The Pico 4 is SUCH a disappointment
author: @christopheroconnor4665

text: +1, especially racing sims in VR: AC1, ACC, AMS2. Any 2D AAA game work well even on 20XX GPU, since they target PS5/XBOX and therefore are not as demanding.
author: @MrVkNext

text:
@christopheroconnor4665  Ehh.

Displayport is one of the worst plugs for a VR headset.  It's probably the worst thing about the Reverb G2.

It's heavy with a stiff cable and doesn't tolerate movement very well.  Newer displayport is just going to be even more sensitive in this regard and come with a shorter cable.

I would prefer usb-c, but honestly, with active cables coming in the new standard that are likely to share displayport's sensitivity, going wireless might actually be a good thing.

text:
@shippy1001  Of course I can blame Nvidia, and their customers, lol. Same how I will always shit on Apple, or Intel, or any other for bad practices.
 
"Don`t get too caught up with the PCIe5.0"
 Anything the card can do can be rendered moot if it cannot transfer data in and out as fast as it needs. I don't think it reached the pcie4 cap yet, but the fact that this technology exists on the market and you're paying a premium to be left out is quite a thing. Also it can be potentially limiting in the near future.

 "no need for DP"
 Again, paying a premium for less commonly used features. This is the same argument people use about Apple on basic functionality that they remove or fail to add in. Like you said, there is a good chance there will be a 4090ti with DP, and so many people will pay the premium-premium for that basic functionality.
 There is no reasonable argument against it, aside from "Nvidia wants more money", which is literally arguing against your interests.

 
 "which is not the case if you are cutting the time in half"
 The argument was productivity. The only reason a company or person would want to invest in upgrading their hardware to be more productivity is to... well, produce more. Doing the same amount of work in less time is meaningless if you're not using that extra time to produce even more. If your 3090s are running 6 hours per day, you want your 4090s running 6 hours per day, pumping out more projects, therefore increasing profits and positively impacting your SLA.
 Therefore, yes, the 4090s WILL increase your cost in electricity. If that increase is less than the extra profit, then it's a good investment. If not, then it's not. On the other hand, if you can't fill up that extra time and therefore is looking at how to save cost in electricity, you're probably not big enough to have such high electricity costs to justify the upgrade.
 Of course, this all depends on the specifics, but my point being is that the 4090 isn't a "no-brainer" just because "big card goes brrrrrrr". 
 And yes, YOU DO care about energy costs. Energy costs are one of the main factors for any computer related operation, and they skyrocket as you go up. Not to mention, the cost isn't linear, since after a threshold you have to incur higher costs to create the infrastructure to feed that much power, even more so if you consider local regulations. Cryptominers often undervolted their cards exactly for this reason.

 And yes, they will be out-of-stock. Nvidia already declared that they are putting inventory in a tight leash. However that doesn't make it a no-brainer nor this god-send of a product.

@lizardpeter  $1600 for a piece of hardware that's going to be bought by a lot less people than you think. Titan and 90 cards are not and never have been reasonable for anyone below prosumer level, given literally no one below that level needs even close to that level of performance.

Basically the groups of people that can actually make use of all that power are three- people with $20k+ gaming setups with high resolution, high refresh rate monitors (which, notably, is actually a WEAKNESS of the 4090 as stated in the video, due to the lack of DP2.0 support), people with badass workstation PCs built for editing, rendering, etc., and people doing heavy-duty AI work. All incredibly small portions of the overall market. And for that middle group, if they upgraded any time in the past three years, they're probably not upgrading to a 4090.

I made the comparison to halo cars for a reason- all told the actual market for these insanely powerful cards is very small, but big numbers make company look good. No average sports car driver is going and buying a Ford GT or Audi R8- not a NEW one, anyway. Same goes for GPUs. The vast majority of the sales these companies make come from their 70-equivalents and lower.

Also, to clarify my point regarding horrific thermals, I was specifically referring to the fact that the 4090 is basically a glorified space heater with how much power it consumes, and its record-setting cooler size. With higher electricity prices and hotter summers, that's... not great at all.
author: @Hexagonaldonut

text:
@lizardpeter  Ignoring the fact that I never used "overkill" specifically, no one is buying these high refresh rate monitors you just listed off. Odds are very few people will be buying a lot of them, because framerate has severely diminishing returns past a certain point. 60 is and has been the generally accepted standard for framerate for years, and even if that does change it's unlikely to go any higher than 120. There's a little thing called "diminishing returns" that comes into play with any framerate higher than 60.

And, no, I'm not citing 60 because that's the standard- though it IS for a reason- but because that's literally about how fast our brains process vision, likely plus or minus a couple Hz on a per-person basis. There's not really much of a benefit to outspeeding your own ability to process images, besides making your numbers bigger.

By definition, anything that can meet the expected minimum- in this case 60 FPS- is not underpowered. And most cards from the past 6-8 years can pull that off at 1080p on even the newest games. (My 970 was only just starting to fall behind this year before I replaced it.)

And while I'm at it I might as well address the giga resolution issue in the room- 1440p will probably become more common, but as-is on typical monitor sizes anything past that loses a lot of benefit. You'd basically need to have your face right up against the monitor to see any benefit, and needless to say that's a bad idea. Accordingly it's exceedingly unlikely 4K will ever see widespread adoption in the conventional monitor space, beyond especially large ones, unless 4K becomes so cheap that it just replaces 1080p wholesale; possible, but unlikely to happen anytime soon. TVs, however, can absolutely leverage the extra resolution afforded by 4K and up, which is why the adoption there has. Actually been surprisingly high, honestly. Point being pixel density isn't beneficial past a certain point, but unlike with framerate there is actually a solution to that: just make the panel bigger.

tl;dr: the big numbers are self-wankery and have very little benefit to anyone besides corporate executives' wallets and those who have really big TVs. Gee, this is kind of reminding me of that car comparison again...

text: The price of transistors has stopped going down a few years ago. It's why the XboneX and PS4 Pro never got a price cut and Microsoft preemptively released their budget Series X as a cut down Series S. (They lose money on both btw) There is only so much you can do with optimizing how the architecture is laid out to squeeze performance out of the same cost chip. These aren't bargain cards. Bargain cards don't play modern games at high settings at high resolutions and refresh rates. It's why low settings exist, and you can thank the industry for making it so low settings don't destroy the look and feel of modern titles. You don't need to play Cyberpunk at Ultra RT 1440p or 4k to enjoy it. I played it on high 1080p on my 1660TI and it was perfectly smooth and honestly outside of RT reflection heavy scenes I can't tell the difference between that and ultra settings in normal gameplay. The bell curve doesn't maximize value at the xx70 class cards anymore. They are more in the 50 to 60 range now. The PS5 has a 3070 class graphics chip that targets 4k and will be around for atleast 6-7 more years. Get a 3050 TI or 3060 and honestly you could run high or ultra on most games till the PS6 launches if you are gaming at 1080p. A 3060 is $380 at my local store, that's only like 50 bucks more than the 1660TI which was considered a value king and will run anything. If you are willing to upgrade in 4 years instead of 6 you could get a 3050 for sub $300 right now.

text:
@MrBenenator  I get it.  I actually have a 5900x, but then again it’s on an asrock b350 board from about 2018, so I’ve been able to update over time.  My screen is 1080p 144hz.  The next upgrade I’ll do will probably be a bigger 1440p 144hz screen since they are coming down in price.  The way I afford some things though is I resell my old stuff.  For example, if I wanted to go to Intel 13th gen I could probably sell the 5900x for about 300, which would cover a board and a good chunk of an i7.  

But in actuality my upgrade order will probably be monitor, gpu, then platform like cpu ram etc.  Part of the draw of Intel 13th gen is having a current cpu/board and reusing my 32gb ddr4 3200.  Don’t get me wrong I may not need 32gb, but I got a good deal from a friend for 80 bucks and resold my 16gb kit.  So my setup is below.  Keep in mind I’ve been upgrading over the last 4-5 years a bit at a time.

5900x
AsRock ab350 pro 4 motherboard 
32gb gskill trident 32gb(4 8gb sticks)
240gb Samsung 960 evo nvme drive.  (This is at least 3-4 years old)
2 1tb sata ssd drives
1 2tb sata ssd drive (got a good deal for just over 100 bucks so didn’t pass it up)
Rx 6700xt (one of the latest additions since prices have started coming down)
Corsair 850 rmx power supply
Cooler master mb511 case with 6 fans
Vetroo v5 tower cooler with 2 fans in push pull setup.

Keep in mind I’ve had this pc since 2018 or so, so I’ve been adding bit by bit.  I will say once you get spoiled to higher refresh rate though you don’t want to go back to a 60 fps screen.  The higher refresh with freesync if you have a decent gpu is nice.  As far as what games I’m playing, playing a lot of total war games lately so the extra cores can help when you are ending your turn and they have multiple factions doing moves.  I did like the spider man game however and the assassin’s creed games up until origin and odyssey.  Maybe I need to revisit those though.

But as for your setup you could definitely go to any ryzen and a decent board and even step up to a cpu like the 5800x3d and be good for a while.

Btw I’m not rich or anything like that, I’m actually a computer tech who happens to enjoy video games.  Thankfully I’ve been able to stretch my budget a little more.  But if I had to be on more of a budget, something like a ryzen 5 3600, decent board, 16gb ram and a card like an rx 6600 for example is perfectly usable.  

If I really had to be on a shoestring budget I’d probably try to pick up either an old pc that my work sometimes sells with an old i7 and upgrade the ram and drop in an ssd, then a budget card like a 1070 or something.  Actually had a gtx 1060 3gb for part of the shortages before I got the 6700xt.

text:
@riazulrahil  People do, actually. Only about 20% or less bother with the rest, look it up. 
You dont actually seem to know how GPU's work, nor how making them works either so i'll do you a favour and explain some basics.

1. AMD came late to the market, and was already at a deficit having fallen under when Intel cracked the single-core market open and took the lead.
The reason AMD is superior in workstation cpu's now, is precisely because they didnt give up the idea of a fast multi-core cpu. They've mastered that art now which is why we see their focus shift in the 7000 series to single core performance, while maintaining their multi-core at a marginal increase over the last gen.
2. Due to the fact that AMD was late to GPU architecture they have had to make sacrifices in their first generations in order to compete in certain categories. This didnt work for the generations before 6000 series GPU's at all, as Nvidia was ahead by a big margin. But in the 6000 series we see them take a lead in many categories with pure rasterization (which was their goal) - later their DLSS alternative has also gotten better and thanks to their stronger rasterization performance the gpus are at least comparable to their 3000 series counterparts. (minus the very top end, as the 3090Ti pulls ahead slightly)

Now, the 3rd and last point is your impression that AMD will never compete in terms of workstation GPU's with Nvidia, but that's outright wrong and cynical. Looking at AMD's history they are far more likely to fix their mistakes rather than not going through every generation, will it be with RDNA2? we'll see. But AMD is certainly capable, and singing NVIDIA's praises does literally NOTHING for you here, we WANT competition. Not to shill for anti-consumer companies who will do anything to try and milk our wallets.

I think AMD is capable, im ready to be disappointed but Im also optimistic about what we'll see with AMD's next generation of GPU's. I think you'd be best in doing the same.
